title: Hidden fluid mechanics: Learning velocity and pressure fields from flow visualizations
authors_full: Maziar Raissi, Alireza Yazdani, George Em Karniadakis
affiliations: Division of Applied Mathematics, Brown University, Providence, RI, USA (all three authors); NVIDIA Corporation, Santa Clara, CA, USA (M. Raissi, present address per PMC metadata)
verification: verified in inventory; open-access full text confirmed (PMC PMC7219083 published main text + arXiv:1808.04327v1 full preprint PDF)
subdomain: inference of hidden velocity/pressure fields from passive-scalar flow visualizations (external flow past cylinder, internal channel flow with stenosis, intracranial aneurysm hemodynamics)
industry_context: Aerodynamics/wind-tunnel testing and clinical hemodynamics (prognosis of heart attack and stroke); funded by DARPA (EQUiPS N66001-15-2-4055, AIRA HR00111990025), AFOSR FA9550-17-1-0013, NIH U01HL142518, DOE (PNNL DE-AC05-76RL01830); author affiliation includes NVIDIA
physics_enforced_exact: Nondimensional passive-scalar transport + incompressible Navier-Stokes + auxiliary complement variable: c_t + u c_x + v c_y + w c_z = Pe^{-1}(c_xx + c_yy + c_zz); d = 1 - c with d_t + u d_x + v d_y + w d_z = Pe^{-1}(d_xx + d_yy + d_zz); u_t + u u_x + v u_y + w u_z = -p_x + Re^{-1}(u_xx + u_yy + u_zz) (and analogous equations for v and w); u_x + v_y + w_z = 0
nonlinearity: strongly nonlinear (convective terms u u_x, v u_y, w u_z in the NS momentum equations; unsteady vortex shedding / Kármán vortex street)
bcs_ic_handled: By design agnostic to geometry, initial and boundary conditions; no velocity/pressure BCs are imposed in general. Exception: a Dirichlet velocity BC is given on the left boundary of the training domain containing the cylinder (2D external flow), because concentration observations there lack sufficient gradients. Uniqueness is instead obtained by choosing training domains where the passive scalar has sufficient normal concentration gradients at the boundaries (dc/dn != 0), which lets the algorithm infer zero velocity on walls with no explicit no-slip BC; the auxiliary variable d = 1-c helps detect the geometry and training-domain boundaries. DNS data generation used realistic BCs (uniform free stream U_inf=1, zero-pressure outflow, periodic top/bottom; pulsatile inflow waveform Q(t) and 'Windkessel' pressure for the aneurysm); pressure BC set to zero in the channel DNS
enforcement_mechanism: soft-penalty (PDE residuals added as squared errors to the data-misfit loss; no hard constraints)
enforcement_details: A deep net maps (t,x,y,z) to (c,u,v,w,p). Automatic differentiation (TensorFlow, statically compiled computational graph fixed throughout training; chain rule) computes the residual networks e1 (transport residual of c), e2 (transport residual of d = 1-c), e3-e5 (the three NS momentum residuals), e6 (continuity u_x + v_y + w_z); a term not present in the residual contributes zero. Residuals enter the loss as squared errors at collocation/residual points. Pressure is identifiable only up to a constant (incompressible flow). Lift/drag and wall shear stresses are then computed analytically from gradients of the parameterized velocity field (trapezoidal rule / summation for surface integrals)
network_architecture: 'Plain vanilla' fully connected DNN: 10 hidden layers x 50 neurons per hidden layer (6 x 50 = 300 neurons for the hidden layer), shared parameters producing outputs (c, d, u, v, w, p); published version schematized as a physics-uninformed net (t,x,y,z) -> (c,u,v,w,p) followed by a physics-informed deep neural network with outputs e1..e5
activation_function: sin(x) (authors note sin is 'numerically more stable than tanh' for computing the residual networks e_i; stated as a conjecture, not a firm result)
input_representation: (t, x, y) for 2D cases; (t, x, y, z) for 3D cases; no extra features. Variant: streaklines from 1D projections of concentration used in supplementary study (fig. S11, table S4)
output_representation: c (passive-scalar concentration), d = 1 - c (auxiliary complement variable), u, v, w (velocity components), p (pressure, defined up to a constant)
loss_terms: Preprint: SSE = sum_{n=1..N} |c(t^n,x^n,y^n,z^n) - c^n|^2 + sum_{n=1..N} |d(t^n,...) - d^n|^2 + sum_{i=1..6} sum_{n=1..N} |e_i(t^n,...)|^2. Published: MSE = (1/N) sum |c(t_n,x_n,y_n,z_n) - c_n|^2 + sum_{i=1..5} (1/M) sum |e_i(t_m, x_m, y_m, z_m)|^2, with N data points on the concentration c and M residual points 'under our full control' (may differ from data points)
loss_weighting: fixed (all terms equally weighted; no annealing/adaptive weighting scheme stated)
sampling_strategy: Dense point clouds of concentration data scattered in space and time over an arbitrarily chosen training domain; in the preprint, residual points coincide with the training data (paper notes they could differ but 'not pursued'; published version enforces at M residual points and notes mini-batch Adam allows penalizing at 'virtually infinitely' many points). Data sizes: 31 million points (flower-shaped domain downstream of cylinder), 2.8 million (domain containing cylinder), 37 million (3D cylinder), 10 million (2D channel), 29 million (3D aneurysm sac)
optimizer_schedule: Adam only (no L-BFGS mentioned). Preprint details: 250, 500 and 500 epochs at learning rates 1e-3, 1e-4 and 1e-5 respectively (one epoch = one pass through the entire dataset); mini-batch size 10000; total Adam iterations = 1000 x (number of data points / mini-batch size)
training_compute: Single NVIDIA Titan X GPU; every 10 optimizer iterations takes ~1.9 s (2D problems) and ~3.8 s (3D problems) (preprint details)
data_regime: Dense synthetic DNS point clouds of the passive scalar concentration only (millions of points); no observations of velocity/pressure at all in most cases (one Dirichlet inflow velocity condition in the 2D cylinder case); hidden fields recovered physics-only. Noise and low-resolution robustness studied on synthetic data (fig. S6, Fig. 2F/fig. S5); published version adds a da Vinci-inspired 2D flow (Fig. 1)
datasets_used: Self-generated spectral/hp element (NekTar) DNS datasets: 2D flow past circular cylinder Re=Pe=100 (Kármán vortex street); 3D flow past finite-size circular cylinder between parallel plates Re=Pe=100; 2D channel flow over an obstacle/stenosis Re=60, Pe=180 (pulsatile inflow); 3D physiologic blood flow in a patient-specific intracranial aneurysm (ICA, cavernous segment of right internal carotid artery) Re=Pe=98.2 with physiologic flow waveform; da Vinci-inspired 2D geometry (published Fig. 1)
baselines_compared: Reference spectral/hp element DNS solutions (NekTar) for all fields, lift/drag forces and wall shear stresses; internal ablation with vs without auxiliary variable d; qualitative (no numeric) contrast with pure machine learning and pure scientific computing approaches
evaluation_metrics: Relative L2 errors per field (c, u, v, w, p) as functions of time; relative error of learned Reynolds/Péclet numbers vs exact; agreement of lift/drag force frequency and amplitude; wall shear stress magnitude vs spectral solver (with dealiasing needed for the reference)
key_quantitative_results: 2D cylinder, flower domain downstream (31M points): rel. L2 errors approx c = 2-3e-3, u = 0.02-0.06, v = 0.03-0.05, p = 0.1-0.2 over most of the prediction interval, with arbitrary training domain and Dirichlet inflow as the only velocity information | Lift and drag forces on the cylinder: 'excellent agreement' with exact; resulting error within 1% of the test data in frequency and amplitude | Learned parameters, 2D cylinder: Pe learned 92.30 vs exact 100 (rel. error 7.60%), Re learned 92.47 vs 100 (rel. error 7.52%) | 2D channel with stenosis (10M points): Pe learned 178.95 vs 180 (0.58%), Re learned 59.92 vs 60 (0.12%); predicted wall shear stress agrees with spectral solver and is smooth (network gradients analytic) vs aliased numerical differentiation | 3D cylinder (37M points): rel. L2 approx c = 4.2-4.6e-3, u = 0.04-0.06, v = 0.03-0.05, w = 0.3, p = 0.04-0.1 — slightly higher than 2D | 3D intracranial aneurysm sac (29M points): rel. L2 approx c = 0.02, u = 0.2, v = 0.2, w = 0.2-0.3, p = 0.4-0.5 (accurate window 10 <= t <= 25) | Reliability threshold: algorithm breaks down with fewer than 5 time snapshots per vortex-shedding cycle or fewer than 250 spatial points (Fig. 2F, fig. S5); robust to substantial noise (fig. S6) and to streakline-only 1D projections (table S4)
errors_reported: 2D cylinder (flower domain, 31M pts): c ~2-3e-3, u ~0.02-0.06, v ~0.03-0.05, p ~0.1-0.2 rel. L2; lift/drag error within 1% of test data | 2D cylinder (domain incl. cylinder, 2.8M pts): u ~0.01, v ~0.03-0.04, p ~0.04-0.05 rel. L2 | Learned Re/Pe: cylinder Pe 92.30/100 (7.60%), Re 92.47/100 (7.52%); channel Pe 178.95/180 (0.58%), Re 59.92/60 (0.12%) | 3D cylinder (37M pts): c ~4.2-4.6e-3, u ~0.04-0.06, v ~0.03-0.05, w ~0.3, p ~0.04-0.1 rel. L2 | 2D channel (10M pts): c ~1e-3, u ~0.02-0.03, v ~0.03-0.05, p ~0.05-0.15 rel. L2 | 3D aneurysm (29M pts): c ~0.02, u ~0.2, v ~0.2, w ~0.2-0.3, p ~0.4-0.5 rel. L2 (values read from figure error curves; approximate)
speedup_claims: No numeric speedups stated. Qualitative claims: HFM yields 'computationally efficient and fully differentiable surrogates' for velocity and pressure; assuming unknown geometry, reproducing the results with conventional solvers would require 'significantly more expensive optimization problems' (parametrized ICs/BCs, backpropagation through solvers or Bayesian optimization), and geometry parametrization would require grid regeneration, 'which makes the approach almost impractical'
ablations: With vs without auxiliary variable d = 1-c: d improves prediction accuracy at 'no additional cost' (figs. 4, 14) and helps detect geometry/training-domain boundaries | Architecture: deeper/wider networks more expressive but costlier; sin(x) vs tanh(x) — sin numerically more stable for residuals (authors' conjecture, reader encouraged to experiment via released code) | Resolution study, six space/time resolutions (Fig. 2F, fig. S5): breaks down below 5 snapshots/vortex-shedding cycle or 250 spatial points | Noise robustness (fig. S6) | Streakline (1D projection) input instead of full 3D concentration (fig. S11, table S4) | Training-domain choice arbitrary downstream of cylinder | BC on cylinder wall c=0 vs dc/dn=0 both effective | Anisotropy/capabilities of residual collocation decoupled from data points discussed but not pursued (preprint)
stated_limitations: Deliberately avoids regimes where Navier-Stokes becomes chaotic/turbulent as Re increases: 'minimizing the loss function (6) might become a challenge', the optimizer 'may fail to converge to the right values', and turbulent inference is left to 'future extensions' (Discussion, preprint p. 26) | Training data on the passive scalar are synthetically generated, 'relatively noiseless and clean compared to realistic measurements' | 3D reconstruction of a passive scalar from a stack of 2D projections is 'not a common practice' clinically due to technological complexities and processing costs; extracting information from 2D images directly (projection angle) is more realistic | Imaging modalities differ in spatial/temporal resolution; for temporal resolution, high-order time-stepping (e.g. implicit Runge-Kutta) resolving equations with very few snapshots is proposed for future work | Predictions weaker at initial and final time instants due to lack of data (weaker if trained on c for t < 0 or t > 16) | Newtonian, incompressible flow assumed (non-Newtonian/compressible extensions sketched, constitutive law could be learned)
failure_modes: Resolution breakdown threshold: fewer than 5 time snapshots per vortex-shedding cycle or fewer than 250 points in the spatial domain (published main text, Fig. 2F) | Error spikes near initial and final time instants of the prediction interval (data sparsity at interval ends) | Expected failure of loss minimization / optimizer non-convergence in turbulent regimes (authors' concern, citing their deep hidden physics models work) | Reference spectral WSS estimates suffer from aliasing/noisy oscillations needing dealiasing, while the network prediction is smooth (instructive contrast on numerical differentiation noise)
reproducibility: All data and code publicly available on GitHub: https://github.com/maziarraissi/HFM (code + data; Zenodo 10.5281/zenodo.3566161) and https://github.com/alirezayazdani1/HFM (synthetic data generators; Zenodo 10.5281/zenodo.3567215); implemented in TensorFlow (static computational graph); published supplementary materials PDF; no random seeds stated
quotable_finding: Specifically, the algorithm breaks down if for training there are fewer than five time snapshots per vortex shedding cycle or fewer than 250 points in the spatial domain. (p. 1028)
relevance_rqs: RQ1: flagship inverse data-assimilation application in fluids & biomedical hemodynamics (heart attack/stroke prognosis, wall shear stresses) | RQ2: loss design (data term + 5 PDE residual terms), auxiliary variable d = 1-c, sin activation, Adam-only schedule, million-point data regime | RQ3: soft-penalty autodiff residuals of NS + transport; BC-free assimilation enabled by normal concentration gradients | RQ4: explicit reliability envelope (resolution/noise breakdown thresholds, turbulence exclusion) - directly quotable for the reliability discussion
manuscript_section: S5 domain applications (fluids/biomed); S4 methods (loss/enforcement mechanism, passive-scalar input representation); T1 domain-application table; T3 reliability/limitations table; F2 loss-design figure
cross_paper_links: builds-on: PINN-A01 (Raissi, Perdikaris, Karniadakis, JCP 2019 'Physics-informed neural networks' = ref. 5 of published version; preprint refs [4,5] = PINN part I/II arXiv:1711.10566/1711.10561); builds-on: Raissi 'Deep hidden physics models' arXiv:1801.06637 and 'Hidden physics models' JCP 357 (2018) 125-141 (refs [14,18] — source of the turbulence/optimizer-failure concern); data generator: NekTar spectral/hp element solver (Karniadakis & Sherwin, ref [27]); companion: Karniadakis & Triantafyllou 3D wake transition ref [31], Grinberg & Karniadakis Windkessel outflow BC ref [35]
notes_caveats: PDF analyzed in full is arXiv:1808.04327v1 (33 pp, 13 Aug 2018; earlier title 'Hidden Fluid Mechanics: A Navier-Stokes Informed Deep Learning Framework for Assimilating Flow Visualization Data') — the PMC/science.org PDF of the published 5-page version blocks programmatic download, but the complete published main text was read via PMC PMC7219083 HTML; fields filled from the published version where stated, otherwise from the preprint (noted per field). Despite 'real-world applications' framing, every flow is synthetic DNS data: no experimental or patient-measured data are used anywhere; noise robustness is shown only on synthetically noised data. Relative L2 values quoted from figure error curves are approximate (order-of-magnitude). Pressure is only identified up to a constant. Data appetite is very large (10-37M concentration points) - far from sparse-sensor practicality. Published version switched SSE->MSE and introduced separate residual points M. Science page number for quotable_finding estimated from PMC article structure (cylinder-results section). No UQ, no domain decomposition, no transfer learning.
